It is me, sir... it is me who loves you... who serves you faithfully and wholeheartedly... who has never broken even one of your orders! Oh sir... I can’t understand why you did that to me, sir!’

But our officer broke into his thoughts with a voice full of tenderness, mercy and kindness, ‘Naturally, you’re upset at what happened!’

Abu Mohammad did not answer.

‘Oh my brother,’ our officer continued in the same gentle tone which overwhelmed him with love. ‘Both you and I were about to fall into a dangerous trap and inevitable disaster; so to avoid that danger and put an end to the impending sedition in the castle and, too, because of the craftiness and spite of the officers who tried to discredit me I was obliged to do what I did.’

Our man kept talking to Abu Mohammad in a friendly way until he made him forget all his bad feelings. Then he brought out two golden liras from his pocket and gave them to him, moreover he gave him one month’s leave with his salary fully paid.

Abu Mohammad opened his eyes and showed his pleasure and satisfaction. His lively voice clearly expressing his renewed high spirits and delight, ‘If that’s how it is sir, then beat me again and give me more golden liras and more leave.’

Our shrewd officer laughed, and there and then Abu Mohammad saluted him and left the officer with a spring in his step.

And so, everything turned out for the best in the castle by virtue of the brilliant conduct of our officer: security and peace prevailed within its walls, and remained thus all during Officer Sheikho’s administration of its affairs.

chapters.title: Occasional Marital Privacy for Prisoners
chapters.html:
Here we tell of another incident during the illustrious career of Officer Amin Sheikho, which is quite different from any of his daring military escapades, and demonstrates a most humane side of his character.

When he held the post of manager of the citadel prison in Damascus, it was customary for family and friends to visit the prisoners on a particular day. On this day, he ordered the prison warders to allow the prisoners’ wives to meet with their husbands privately, for a limited time, in individual rooms. There was no provision made in prison regulations for this relaxing of the rules so the warders disapproved of this move and were extremely resentful to carry out this order. They considered that guarding the prisoners while they were alone with their wives was outside their field of duty and detracted from their own dignity.

Not to be outdone, that noble man, the great officer, took up a firearm and assumed the duty of the simple guard in front of the individual prison rooms which he had assigned for the privacy of the prisoners and their wives. He paced slowly back and forth, back and forth, until visiting time was over, and the prisoners went back to their dormitories. Then he assembled the wardens and addressed them in a stern, commanding tone, ‘I, the manager of the citadel and the prison, have just done your job... the work of the prison warder, and I was proud to do it... I was happy to do what’s right and to help these couple to avoid forbidden acts. From this day on whoever refuses to perform this duty will be strictly penalized.

‘Why do you regard this humane indulgence, which Al’lah has legalised, with contempt? Maybe the husband needs his wife to repair his clothes or to discuss private family matters which they did not want the other prisoners or the jailers to overhear.’

With that, a normal routine was established and they went back to fulfilling this humane assignment, willingly or unwillingly, because they had seen that the commander had shown the way and not been too proud to undertake the job himself.

Officer Mohammad Amin had understood the positive effects of that humane service through his great insight and his illumination by Al’lah’s Light, for there are family matters between a husband and his wife which the prisoner cannot discuss within the sight or hearing of other people present during the communal visit.

Besides, this deed of Officer Sheikho does not conflict with the reason that reformative prisons were established, nor does it disagree with Godly Mercy. In fact, a point that many people forget is that the prison was originally established with the aim of reforming men found guilty of crime, and not for destroying their families and human spirits.

And what is more, not allowing a prisoner to be alone with his wife for a short while can cause moral deterioration, and a terrible lowering of both morals and religious belief, and in many cases, even sexual deviation and the spread of sodomy among the prisoners. On the other hand, this simple connection helps the prisoners to avoid such ugly aberrations and also stops their wives from straying and being tempted to commit adultery during their husbands’ absence and period of incarceration. It builds up hope in their spirits and maintains a strong bond between the prisoner and his family whereby he fully realises the happiness created within the family unit and, hopefully, stops committing any further crimes or disgraceful deeds, and making it so much easier for him to truly repent.

chapters.title: The Irreverent Grocer Is Foiled
chapters.html:
“Truly, the eyes may commit adultery by looking.”

You may wonder, why the Almighty orders us to lower our gaze. We know that adultery is a dangerous social aberration. When it becomes widespread in society, that society will crumble and be destroyed just as the AIDS syndrome devastates a man’s body, rendering it powerless and subject to the slightest infection which will cause it to waste away, depleted and destroyed by the power of the infection.

That critical illness breaks down even the most hallowed social links, as when the first basic cell in the structure of society, the family, deteriorates, it will collapse and be completely destroyed; this is contrary to the bond of marriage which is based upon a proper foundation and the strict rules enacted for us by our Wise and Omniscient Creator.

The fruits of adultery may well be a generation of illegitimate children since there will be no father to acknowledge them, or raise and advise them, therefore they will follow the ways of corruption and wrongdoing through delinquency. Furthermore, it is important to consider the perilous future which the adulteress would suffer, for the adulterer would surely desert her in favour of another woman after her first flush of beauty has waned, leaving her desolate when subjected to the pursuant misery and destitution of her horrible, dreary fate.

And so it is with him, for when he deserts the material life he will have left behind no lasting benefits to society; on the contrary, he will be exposed to the pernicious ailment which arises from such a course. He will be like a destructive pickaxe demolishing the happiness of every woman he may connect with, and at the end of his lifetime he will find no loving child or kindly relative to help him in the twilight of his years. He will certainly suffer from sorrow and burn with misery at the lamentable end of his life. Even if he seeks marriage towards the end of his youth, he will undoubtedly select a maiden since he will have become accustomed to connecting with young girls. Moreover, he will be unlikely to settle for just one woman as he has been used to drinking from different springs, and so his wife might also react to his errant ways after he reaches middle age.

Consequently, problems such as boredom and weariness would arise on both sides, quite apart from the physical diseases stemming from this lowly path which are obvious to everyone; this state often results in divorce. Therefore, and to turn mankind away from following such a course, the Almighty legislates the law for him, since Al’lah’s Religion is a religion of preservation, and as the saying goes, “Prevention is better than cure.” The Almighty says, “Nor come close to adultery”, that is, anything may lead one to commit fornication: speech, song, shaking hands, cinema, radio, looking at women. Just as the eye may provoke adultery, it is the same with the ear and the hand; and all of this may lead man to commit fornication. God continues, “For it is indecent and a bad path.” ﴿150﴾

It leads man to have his offspring through a contemptible way and causes harm to those who commit it.

Al’lah had revealed this wisdom and requested that all mankind should apply this teaching voluntarily, since he who does not comply with it will be ruined. The Almighty shows us that following these unequivocal verses which reveal to us the way to achieve our happiness, will result in our bliss here on this earth and in the Hereafter, when we are amongst the dwellers of Heaven. The Almighty orders us, “Tell the men who are believers that they should lower their gaze and guard their modesty: that will make for greater purity for them; and Al’lah is Well- Acquainted with all that they do.” ﴿151﴾

According to this verse, Al’lah commands us to lower our gaze because the eye can commit adultery simply by looking and then forming impure thoughts; and if a man fails to lower his gaze he will fall into the ways of fornication and lose his discretion. On the contrary, by lowering and averting his sight he will guard his modesty and he will be preserved from falling into the sinful ways of fornication. If he consistently lowers his gaze he will maintain his modesty and love his wife and she, too, will love him.

If mankind does not apply this Instruction given by Al’lah, the Almighty will send them warnings, and cautions, or inflict hardship or distress so that they may understand the error of their ways which lead man to commit fornication.

This incident which occurred with the grocer who rented a shop from Mohammad Amin is a perfect explanation for the saying mentioned above.

Mohammad Amin had inherited this old shop from his late father, and it was situated on the ground floor of the house where the master lived with his small family. The house consisted of two floors, the upper one occupied by the highly-principled man, Mohammad Amin, and his family, and the ground floor which included the shop.

Usually, as Amin Bey passed by, he would see the grocer sitting on a chair at the door of the shop with an open copy of the Holy Qur’an resting in his hands. One would assume that this indicated moral rectitude and presaged that his conduct and behaviour would inevitably conform to the true religion in relation to trustworthiness. Of course, all of this was most desirable if that grocer really had been truly faithful and honest, or even sought Al’lah’s Satisfaction.

But, alas... the reality was different, and as one knows, appearances can be deceptive, which has been proven by fact. It happened one day when the great guide was passing in front of the shop and noticed the grocer’s eyes chasing what Al’lah had forbidden: he was lost in his devilish thoughts and gazing lustfully at a woman walking past the shop, his eyes following her till she faded in the distance. And yet he held the Holy Qur’an open in his hands and then turned back to studying it for all to observe!

And now, in an instant, our great guide had seen him for what he really was: the shopkeeper had fallen into the sin of staring at what Al’lah had forbidden, which would inevitably lead him to something even worse, that is to commit adultery. That honourable man, Mohammad Amin Sheikho, objected to seeing this infringement not only in his neighbourhood, but in his very own shop. He felt a surge of Godly Anger, full of mercy, flowing into every atom of his spirit, mixed with sorrow for this sinner and for the misery he would bring upon himself. This is why he hurried to admonish the shopkeeper so that he might reflect on his mistake and withdraw from his straying and carelessness. Our man hoped that he would convince him to realise the error of his ways and come to his senses to escape from the possible results of this deed, and from the devil’s snares, and avoid the unhappiness and pains he would ultimately incur for himself.

He went up to the shopkeeper and said to him, ‘What have you just done? Is this allowed? Isn’t it incompatible with religion and morals... and with honesty and uprightness?’

Knowing full well what that honest man meant, the wily tradesman replied, ‘What do you mean, Bey?’

The merciful master said, ‘I have seen you looking openly at women... is that acceptable?’

The sly shopkeeper replied, ‘But, surely we’re allowed to look just once... but any further glances will count against us!’

Amin Bey said to him, ‘But it was a long gaze, in fact it took your entire attention. You literally swallowed her with your eyes... Look, man, the eye may commit adultery just by looking, and you are falling deeper into this shameful act... into immorality... I’m telling you now in case you didn’t realise it, otherwise it would be better if you stop sitting there with the Holy Qur’an in your hands, pretending piety and righteousness. As long as you display such hideous deed you may give the wrong impression about the religion. And what’s more, I’m also telling you that the man that is not a strong believer may suppose that your behaviour represents true religion and that all religious men are like you... so, you will only misrepresent and debase the religion and its beliefs.’

One day, not long after this incident, Mohammad Amin happened to notice that a man went into the grocery shop to buy a few items, which he paid for according to the prices shown. Shortly after the man left with his purchases a little girl came in and, by the Wisdom of the Wise, she bought sweet melon for which the stated price was one franc for a kilogram. But the grocer lied and told her that it was two francs for the kilo, that is, he charged her double the price... yes, he had traded on this child’s tender years to make a greater profit.

At this, the spirit of our honest man rebelled: he felt as if every particle of his being was rejecting the state of affairs concerning that dishonest and corruptive man who had withdrawn far from Al’lah. What fate would he face in this life before the heavenly life to come, if he never retreated from his wrongful ways, came to his senses and duly repented?

Mohammad Amin began to chastise him, pointing out the error of his ways, and described to him the gravity of his straying from the right path, so that he might discard the cloak of depravity and Satanism and replace it with the garment of humanity for which he had been born. He said to him, ‘Why did you do that, man? Would you sell your eternal life for this despicable way of life... because you’re earning your daily bread through unlawful means? Isn’t this deceit? Even though the Prophet (cpth) said, “He who cheats can never belong to us”, I saw you take extra money from that innocent child, so tell me isn’t that theft or even usury? Don’t you know that Al’lah abhors it and will ensure that money gained in this way will be lost; and yet He blesses the money given as alms? Won’t you die one day? Do you think this world will last forever? How will you face your Provider, you who pretend to be so pious and upright? What state will you be in?’

But insisting on his errant ways and following his whims, the heartless tradesman replied, ‘Oh, Bey! It’s called trade and trade is based upon craftiness!’

Hereupon, Mohammad Amin realised that such a man would never respond to his admonishments because he was bent on his life of depravation, swindling and pretence. He acted like an infectious disease which would inflict illness on the human body, and when transmitted would impose grave danger on the whole of society.

That is why this virtuous and noble master decided that he ought to tell the underhand merchant to vacate the shop, since he understood full well that gentle words would achieve nothing with him. So, the only solution was for him to leave not only the shop but also the neighbourhood, therefore our honest man felt that he should admonish him directly and forcefully. So, he said, ‘Listen to me, man! I don’t want to see you here tomorrow... get out of my shop today or else I’ll have to treat you severely... and I don’t want to be forced into it... have you understood?’

When the sly shopkeeper heard these words, his heart was overcome with fear; he trembled with terror when he saw this august master appear like a predatory and rapacious lion which it would be foolish to confront. The shopkeeper’s strength failed him and he remained silent. Then he said, ‘At the end of this month, before the rent is due again, I shall empty the shop for you.’ Mohammad Amin departed having warned the tradesman that he would hold him to his word.

That night, a fire broke out in the grocery store and as soon as Mohammad Amin realised what was happening, he dashed down to help to put it out. He rushed out of his house like a whirlwind and found some of the neighbours had quickly gathered to extinguish the fire. It was too late as the flames had incinerated all the goods in the shop leaving nothing but cinders, but strangely enough there was no damage to the wooden ceiling above which was the floor of the honourable master’s house. The reason for this can easily be explained: the source of money from which alms has been paid will never be destroyed.

A fire engine arrived on the scene soon after the fire had been extinguished and a police car went to the grocer’s house to tell him what had happened. No-one had witnessed the occurrence the previous day or overheard Mohammad Amin ordering the grocer to vacate the shop. At that point, extinguishing the fire and the losses of the poor grocer were uppermost on everyone’s minds and there was no suspicion at all as to who might have caused the fire: certainly no-one would have suspected Mohammad Amin.

At the grocer’s home, the policemen knocked at the door, waking him from his sleep. When they informed him of the fire, the news came like a bolt from the blue; he cried, ‘Oh... Oh, no! It’s my own fault... yes, by God, I forgot my cigarette on the block of fat. Oh, what terrible luck! Has everything been destroyed? My losses will be enormous if all my goods have been burnt.’

He kept crying and, in his anguish, repeating himself over and over again, wringing his hands in despair.

In fact, in his distress he was unaware that he was uttering the truth: Al’lah had made him say these words which would acquit the noble master of any wrongdoing, since the suspicion might well have focused on him.

Before the shopkeeper could even think about the previous day’s incident and make use of it maliciously to take revenge by accusing Mohammad Amin of purposely starting the fire, he unwittingly spoke the truth about the cause of the fire. So, he had no chance of changing his mind and accusing him since he had confessed the truth in front of the policemen.

As for the faithful wife of Mohammad Amin, that merciful, tender-hearted mother, she became extremely troubled when she heard about the accident, because of her great concern for her children, especially when she saw the flames and smoke rising from the ground floor and coming through the window. The actual situation, though, was not as bad as she thought. This Wise Godly Measure included His great Goodness for her and for her honest and pure husband, as due to extreme fear for her two sons, she hurried to their room thinking to carry them out to the street; but in her anxiety she forgot to cover her face with her veil and failed to put on her black cape. And yet, the High Omnipotent God arranged a solution... with a difference! Since she was good-hearted and pure, Al’lah preserved her from harm in this dangerous situation because she was horrified and overwhelmed with the fear that her sleeping children might be burnt to death. So, being unable to carry both boys at the same time she quickly carried one of them to another room; but instead of putting him down and returning empty-handed to bring the second child she forgot to put down the first child and he was still in her arms as she went back to get the second son. Such was her state of distress that she put him back where she had taken him from and picked up the second child to remove him to safety in the opposite room. This state of confusion continued for some time as she ran back and forth between the two rooms, moving first one child and then the other, unable to pick up both of them together... her distress mounting with every passing moment as she was convinced that her sons would be harmed.

Finally, the matter came to an end and the fire was put out. When the honest master returned to his house he found her still overcome with worry and entirely exhausted. So, he calmed her fears and told her that the fire had been extinguished without causing any damage to the ceiling of the shop (which was directly below the floor of the house) and that the danger was over, and everything would be fine. In his gentle way he was able to reassure her and she soon returned to her normal tranquil self for the sake of their children.

So, God’s Mercy is given specifically to those who need it, as is His Affliction, as everyone receives what he deserves according to his intentions and deeds whether they be good or bad. If a man intends goodness he will find nothing but goodness, and if he commits evil deeds, he will be afflicted with punishment and chastisement here on this earth and in the Hereafter unless he shows true repentance and returns to his right mind.

Thus, the Wisdom and Compassion of the Wise and Merciful Al’lah were pleased to release this merciful man, Mohammad Amin, who was not accustomed to giving way to lies and leaving them to circulate. On the contrary, he always quashed them most forcefully. Similarly with the residents of the quarter, when they became comfortable with that licentious, depraved and corruptive man, Al’lah rid them of his wrongdoing by imposing appropriate sanctions so that he might learn to refrain from his careless perfidy, come back to his right mind and correct his sinful ways before it became too late and he forfeited his eternal life. On the other hand, Al’lah had protected our virtuous and pure master, and his wife, from every evil, when the ceiling of the shop was not damaged and prevented her from going out, unveiled, to the street and erroneously show herself to the people outside.

Al’lah had saved her and her honest husband from that difficult situation in order to preserve the purity of them both, and for the honour of her great husband (God sanctified his lofty secret and eternal support).

chapters.title: Prisoner in the Castle or Guest of Honour?
chapters.html:
The incidents described here took place when Officer Mohammad Amin held the position of director of Damascus Castle during the French Mandate over Syria. This vast castle contained an extensive prison full of those who had broken the law, and arsenals stocked with large amounts of weapons and military equipment belonging to the French government which ruled our countries at that time. So, the preparation for war and equipping the armies with war material and provisions were managed in this castle by its director-general Mohammad Amin Sheikho. He was in charge of all its departments and affairs and therefore responsible for despatching the troops from there.

As one can see, our officer held a considerable post in the government, and a castle of such importance should definitely be directed by a man who was worthy of having such a high level of responsibility and trust placed in his hands. Therefore, our officer was always charged with those weighty, critical tasks which required a strong character and great wisdom and acumen to fulfill them successfully.

The ruling class at that time would resort to him for help with the many varied problems which they were unable to solve, whether within the castle or beyond its walls, and indeed in all of Damascus. Needless to say, our officer resolved all problems perfectly. Therefore they called him ‘Aslan’ ﴿152﴾

, a nickname by which he had long been known, because of their affection for him and their admiration of his humane accomplishments and his great integrity: it was as if he was the leader and they were his followers.

For this reason, there were many men who were jealous and harboured feelings of ill-will towards him. They did not like his truthfulness and loyalty so they did their best to destroy the man who stood as a stronghold against the tottering towers of their disbelief and transgressions, and eradicated their dreams and greed, thus putting an end to the outcomes of their evil and wrongful deeds. They constantly tried to undermine his excellent character by spreading doubts about his honesty and his capacity to be the director, and hatching all manner of plots against him. Had he fallen foul of even one of those plots, his fate would have been either exile or capital punishment. But the Almighty was always his Protector. He supported him by giving him power and authority and directed him towards the performing of good deeds and successful tasks that helped to protect him and maintain his prestige.

This story demonstrates to us a lamentable fact which affirms that the man who turns away from God will live in constant misery and darkness. He will spend his life as though blind and deaf, unable to see the light or hear the truth, until he ends up at a level lower than that of an animal and more distant than that of the devil; unless my Lord should feel fit to bestow His Mercy.

One of the adjutants who worked with Officer Mohammad Amin is an example: his heart became entirely controlled by the devil when he adopted a hostile attitude towards our officer. The devil began to support him in weaving schemes and plots against the honest officer, and making his bad deeds and wrongdoing seem right and fair to him. He also raised in him false hopes for a life full of fulfillment and glory, but one achieved in entirely the wrong way. Thus, this man became a real source of evil and began to spread corruption throughout the land by any means possible. Step by step, he gave himself up to the devil and turned into a weapon in the demon’s hands to fulfill his purpose in misleading the sons of Adam and driving them away from the sources of good, truth and honest pleasure. The adjutant’s heart became a mass of bitter rancour and hatred.

Whenever he saw anyone enjoying some special favour, he wanted to have it for himself; in fact, he wished to possess everything the earth had to offer in the way of pleasure, grace and treasure, so as to use or dispose of it however he wished. His self-love was paramount to him; he could not deprive himself of its low desires which overwhelmed him and settled in his debased heart. As a result, he lived in absolute darkness and his heart grew ever darker until eventually he came to loathe kindness and goodwill. His worldly desires obscured the light which enabled him to see the truth, so he became unable to distinguish between good and evil, and never hesitated to fulfill all that his sick whims and impulses desired.

‘Why not? Why couldn’t I be the overlord of this generation? Couldn’t I become a famous personality whose name will go down in history? But what about that man, Officer Sheikho? He puts me in the shade. His character and abilities are far superior and greater than mine. He’s the only obstacle standing in my way. I shall do whatever it takes to destroy him. I’m so envious of all that he has and is!’

This man then took full advantage of every opportunity that presented itself to defame the character of Officer Mohammad Amin whom he believed stood in the way of his future development and happiness. So, he became preoccupied with telling lies and making up false accusations about him, in an attempt to slander his habitual honesty and the purity of his good name. Because of his insistence on evil, Al’lah the Almighty actually gave him the power to bring out the mean wishes which filled his spirit and were written on his heart, and so he wandered too far off the right path. He lived in an ivory palace built by his own dreams and covetousness, which had taken control of him, and which he believed would raise him to a high position of authority and glory.

Nevertheless, the Will of God (Glory to His Names) and the rule of compassion which He decreed Himself and which overwhelms all His creatures, prescribed the help these people needed to turn away from this terrible path which would lead them to a horrible end at the time of their death. His Clemency and Tenderness require that anyone that mistakes his own goodness should be alerted to the error of his ways and warned of the outcomes of his tyranny which will cause him nothing but failure and misery, surely to be followed by total loss and remorse. Therefore He directs distress and misfortune towards him in order to turn him from his lowly desires and whims. If he, when calamity strikes, realises his sins and the enormity of the error of his ways, he should then resort to God and pray to him truthfully. He would then advance on a journey of repentance seeking God’s Forgiveness, by being attached to the cords of sincerity which would reveal to him the reality of this world and the dirtiness of his deeds, as they would acquaint him with God’s Mercy and abundant Favour given to him and, indeed, to all His creatures.

That is what happened with the adjutant of whom we speak, whose greediness and shunning of what is right, grew until the desire for the material things of life captivated his heart, so he mounted the wings of his imagination and instead of soaring high as a bird, he descended from one level of darkness to another, all the while thinking that he could reach the moon and become the focus of all eyes. But suddenly, his self-conceit broke, his pride vanished, and his ivory palace fell down around him, throwing him into a bottomless pit. He was hoisted with his own petard. The arrow which he had fired to hit the great heart of this officer turned back to hit him, even though that heart of that officer wished for him nothing but good and prayed only for his proper guidance and infinite happiness in this world and the world to come.

He said to himself, ‘Woe betide me! Soon I’ll be captured by Officer Sheikho; I have no pistol and am powerless... I’ll surely be convicted because of my crime and evil deeds. What’s more, I was hostile towards him and lost no opportunity to speak badly about him. Oh, I wish I had the power to kill him! But no! I will not give in to fear and desperation. I have to persevere and screw up my courage to be able to meet him and face up to his assault.’

And so, that disastrous night, when that miserable man was arrested in the very act, was the worst night of his life. He was taken to a filthy, dark cell in the police station before being driven to the prison in Damascus Castle to spend the period of his sentence. There were many hundreds of prisoners and criminals in that huge prison, criminals who had been brought from all parts of the Damascus region and its environs.

The time dragged by so slowly as he sat miserably in the middle of the room on a rickety wooden bench covered with a dirty, worn rug. A dim light penetrated the only filthy window high in the wall, drawing on the ground the fearful black shadow of a prisoner; outside could be heard the sound of the slow, measured footfall of the guard who paced back and forth. In his isolation, this sound unnerved him and roused him to a violent reaction within himself. An icy coldness began to creep into his bones. It was the coldness of his feelings of loneliness, and his fear of the approaching hardships which he anticipated living under, and in which he felt as though he were about to be buried alive. His teeth chattered and his body trembled as he looked at his feet and almost felt the severe pains he would suffer. He imagined them swollen and encircled by drops of his own warm blood, and a cold sweat broke out on his pale forehead. His black shadow drawn on the floor of the cell reminded him of his dark, churlish deeds and a loud cry issued from him and resounded in the room, ‘Go away! I don’t want to see you. Go away, you cursed blackness. You remind me of myself. I’m suffering enough distress.’

That is the state of anyone who shuns God. His dark deeds cling to him like a shadow, depriving him of sleep and embittering his life. They keep reminding him of the blackness of his heart and the darkness of his grave.

The prisoner had no relief from this state until eventually he became exhausted by his imagination and obsessed by his fear of the suffering to come. So, he lay down trying to relax... trying to sleep so that he might forget the situation he was in and the horrible visions which shared his loneliness and did away with his peace and tranquillity. But as soon as he closed his eyes, he felt as though he were being whipped severely without mercy; so, he started trembling and moved away from that ill-omened bench. He looked around the room but found no-one except that accursed black shadow. He talked to it, but it gave no reply. He shouted at it, but in vain. So, he decided to ignore it and began to walk around the cell, dragging his tired legs, trying to brace his spiritual powers in order to stay firm and not to break down.

‘Oh God! What’s the matter with me? Have I lost my mind? Couldn’t I stay strong and control myself? I shouldn’t care about being sentenced to a term in prison. Imprisonment denotes manhood. I counted all the costs before I committed that crime, so I was fully aware of the possible consequences and knew that if I was found out I would be arrested and sent to prison for a while; I was prepared to put up with that for the sake of achieving my many wishes... so why am I so afraid? I don’t know why I feel such a sense of mounting horror and cowardice. I see myself as weak-hearted! But no... I’m not! I should control myself. It is only for a short time... some days or months at the most. Yes, I’ll be patient until it’s over.’

He continued to mutter these statements to himself to relieve his fear and concern, but when he remembered that his name was listed with those to be sent to the castle where our officer Mohammad Amin was the director, he lost his mind and became terribly anxious and confused once again, ‘But, will that man leave me alone? I don’t think so. No doubt he’ll seize the opportunity to inflict all kinds of torture on me because I wronged him and did my best to outdo him and disgrace him. I’m sure that he won’t lower himself to forgive me; of course, he won’t, he’ll even use his position to destroy me and to make me serve as a lesson for everybody. Yes, I’m sure Officer Sheikho will use the lash on me; he’ll probably shave my hair and pull out my nails. My back will be ripped and he’ll scar my skin with his cigarette butts... I’ll lose everything: my health, my youth and my name.’

While enveloped in that black state of hysteria, a strong feeling of dizziness overcame him and he felt as if the ground shook beneath his feet. Wherever he moved he saw his shadow following him, provoking him. He boiled with uncontrollable rage and gnashed his teeth... and then he walked slowly towards the wall to kill that black picture and toss it on the floor. He thought that he could wipe it out, so he kicked the wall, then punched it, but to no avail. Finally, he found himself at the end of his tether, so he surrendered to it and accepted its existence. He knew that there would be no escape from his punishment and there was nothing he could do except face up to it and patiently bear his suffering.

‘It is my past history which I created by my own actions... my own terrible deeds. I have done many bad things in my life. Firstly, I wronged myself and then I took every opportunity to do evil and tell lies. How many nights have I lain awake, planning and scheming? How many days have I spent searching and asking? How many doors have I knocked at? How many clubs and coffeehouses have I visited so as to be on good terms with certain people and be accepted by them? It is my own tongue which spoke the words, and my pen which wrote them. Oh God! Isn’t there any way for me to get out of all of this? Isn’t there any way for me to feel at ease or to sleep? Oh God! Please help me; I can’t stand up any more. Oh my God! Please show me Your Mercy. I wish to God I had died before this disaster. Death would be easier than the shame which I will feel when I stand before Officer Mohammad Amin, in chains and humbled, my eyes looking down.’

Before continuing this story, let us study the reason that caused this guilty prisoner to suffer such deep anxiety and terrible feelings, and the fearful prospect of the outcome which he had drawn in his mind. Definitely, he knew that he had been wrong and unjust, just as he knew for certain that the reasons for his actions were certainly not good.

He remembered how he had stood against all that was right in order to achieve his personal aims and gain advantages. He turned to libelling the good reputation of that pure man, Officer Mohammad Amin, and his social standing among his superiors; furthermore, he tried to implant doubts about his high honour and noble intentions. He did all that because Officer Sheikho stood in his way and stopped his wrongdoing.

Our officer feared no-one in his endeavours to establish justice. He did not hesitate for a single moment in performing all that his true love for God and his caring about the advantages for His creatures inspired him to do. He thought of himself as being in charge of protecting people and helping them to follow the way of the most beloved of all Prophets and the imam of all men, our pure and great master Mohammad (cpth).

Therefore, our compassionate man, Mohammad Amin, always refused all requests ﴿153﴾

made by such people because he knew of the bad outcome for the person himself, as well as for the whole of society in general. How many times had he taken the side of the persecuted against those who unjustly used their power and influence? So, through his mercy he interrupted the course of the greediness of this man who now became a prisoner, for Mohammad Amin cared about what was right for him and refused his evil requests. Yet the man regarded this as an insult, so he decided to fight him and even try to kill him. But now, since this sinner had admitted to himself that truly he was at fault and that all his claims were baseless, and in fact it was his own whims and lust which had engulfed him and made him lose sight of the right way, he realised that the officer would be right to punish him and take his revenge. This is what made him so terrified and caused such fearful thoughts to flood his imagination, to the point that he wished he could die rather than meet face to face with Officer Sheikho, the general manager of the castle and its prison.

In the meantime, the daily list of names of the new prisoners arrived at the castle at the normal time, and Mohammad Amin, as usual, sat at his desk in the director’s office and began to read the list to see if he recognised any of the names. Suddenly, a wonderful gleam came to his pure eyes when he saw the name of a certain man. He knew he was not wrong! He wondered about it, then said to himself, ‘Oh you low life! So, your dirty wheels have run their course and carried hundreds of losers with you, clinging to your back! And here is one of those whom you rejected and tore into with your claws! And now he’s to be brought to my castle and come under my control which, surely, never crossed anyone’s mind!’

So, this majestic, imposing castle is about to witness a new battle with a prisoner who has been entrusted to the merciful care of Officer Sheikho and will be enveloped in his noble, superior intentions. Sweet tears of joy flowed from the eyes of our noble officer as he breathed a deep, fragrant sigh of relief, and his affectionate voice quivered with statements of praise and immense gratitude directed towards this Grand God Who was overwhelming him with love and tenderness.

‘How Merciful You are, my God! Despite the fact that he has distanced himself from You, and despite his fight against right, and his wrong to himself, You did not close the doors of love and forgiveness in his face... in fact, I see him as more fortunate than anybody else as he is about to receive a great share of Providence and good fortune. Who would believe that fate has led him here? What a great surprise! I think that he must be in a state of shock now. He probably thinks that I am very happy because of his situation and cannot wait to take my revenge on him. Poor man! He may be trembling with fear, ashamed and suffering from great anxiety. Oh what a poor man!’

Signs of Holy Love and Clemency appeared on Mohammad Amin’s face while a pleasant smile appeared on his lips expressing his pleasure and endless praise to God for this opportunity which He had given to him.

Anxious to put his merciful plan into action, he called the gendarmes, and in no time, three of them entered the office. They were faithful to him and captivated by his noble character which overwhelmed them with the great care and interest he showed each of them. Countless times he had helped them to live in peace, far from falling foul of the danger lurking either within the castle or beyond it.

He told them, ‘Tomorrow, the castle will be honoured by the visit of a man who is dear to us. I’ve decided to receive him as a guest to spend some time here in our castle. So, you have to prepare the best room in the castle, paying particular attention to its location, outlook and size. I want it to be furnished with luxurious furniture. Clean it from top to bottom and paint the walls bright white. Don’t forget to put pots of flowers and greenery in the corners to brighten them. Ensure that it’s provided with every possible convenience and good lighting by which he’ll be able to relax both day and night. It will be a good idea to cover the floor with beautiful, high quality carpets. In short, I want you to prepare a wonderful room, and I want it to be finished today. Off you go... quickly... and make sure that the room is ready for receiving the important guest.’

They saluted him respectfully then rushed off to decide which room would meet all the specifications listed by their hospitable commandant. They divided the work among themselves: one brought the paint and began to paint the walls energetically while another started to sweep and wash the floors.

When they had completed these preparations they went to bring luxurious pieces of furniture and arrange them in the room in the most elegant and comfortable way. And finally, they brought the carpets and the planters containing displays of greenery and beautiful roses which completed the perfect overall appearance of the room.

And so, with the willing gendarmes put to work all was accomplished within a few hours and everything was arranged in the best possible way. Then, one of the gendarmes headed for Mohammad Amin’s office to tell him that the room was ready for his inspection and give his approval. Our officer went up to the room which was situated in the tower. During his inspection, he noticed a few small imperfections that did not meet with his excellent taste and exacting standards. Once these had been put to right, he set off on his usual thorough inspection of the castle and to check the conditions of the prisoners, to be sure that all his orders had been carried out according to the smallest detail. Then, this shining example of leadership and dignity returned to his office and sat looking forward to the arrival of the “special guest” so as to receive him personally with great hospitality and all due attention.

Dear reader, do you think this is an exaggeration or that it is just an ingenious trap set by the director for him to sneer at this prisoner and then change his tactics to torture him?

As for the prisoner, he spent a sleepless night, groaning and suffering the most terrible bouts of fear. Whenever he felt that the time to leave for the castle approached he became even more anxious and alarmed. He felt as though he was living a horrible nightmare from which he would never wake up. With the dawn of the new day, he felt that he could no longer think or feel anything. When the policeman came to take him away he stretched his hands out to be shackled and followed him with heavy, shuffling steps. The patrol wagon was waiting beside the police station in front of the court in al-Marjah Square, Damascus, and it was filled with prisoners to be driven to the castle. His spirits fell even further as he climbed in to join them.

The wagon trundled slowly on its way, laden with two things: the exhausted hearts of the men it was transporting and the huge wheels which, with every turn, drew ever deeper lines in the hearts of those poor men that they would never forget. In fact, it was they themselves who had etched those lines through their own mean deeds which had caused them this hardship. Every one of them was looking through the bars of the wagon, their sorrow clear to see as they bid goodbye to their freedom and the wonderful light of day; as the wagon rolled ever closer to the citadel they endeavoured to remember the sight of everything they passed: houses and streets, people walking by, and leave behind them the happy memories of their past.

But! What brought you to such a situation?

Do you not have eyes to see with?

Do you not have ears to hear with?

Has Al’lah not given you hearts for you to be aware of reality?

Oh that poor son of Adam! When he is enjoying good health and youth, he forgets that he is a weak creature who cannot do without his Creator. He becomes conceited, full of himself, and preoccupied with his wealth and youth so he lives this life as he pleases, trying to gain people’s gratification and not God’s Satisfaction. He follows only what is to his own advantage, even if that makes him go against what is right and rebel against high principles. And so, he sinks ever deeper into a mire of dirt until the day comes when God removes his will and his power in a blink. On that day, he will no longer be able to do anything for himself. He will be put in his coffin and then be carried on sturdy shoulders to be driven to the grave, to return to the soil from which he was created. Then, the list of his works, good and bad, will be shown to him to throw him into a pit of contrition and regret.

When the wagon reached the entrance of the castle, the prisoners got down with pain in their hearts, their heads bowed. They stood in a long line in the great courtyard while gendarmes stood on both sides waiting for the list of names to be read out: each prisoner would be assigned to a particular, numbered cell where he would stay for the period of his sentence. There were various types of prisons in the huge castle depending on the different judgements and sentences handed out. The cells in the tower were usually assigned to those who had committed relatively minor misdemeanors where the sentences were short-term of one year or less. Those prisons were comparatively good in comparison with the others, which were very harsh and more effective on the spirits of the prisoners who were there for long sentences, sometimes even with added penal servitude, that is, “prisons within prisons”.

So, during his sentence, every prisoner had to pass through various difficult circumstances until he became used to a harsh way of life, the face of the jailer became familiar to him, and he accepted loneliness as his only constant friend until God’s Relief finally came.

After the list was read out, the prisoners were led by the guards to their assigned cells. Some were taken to solitary cells, others to collective ones. As for those sentenced to death or to life or long-term imprisonment, that is people who had committed serious felonies and acts of depravity, they were taken to the castle, while the prisons in the towers were the place for those who had committed simple misdemeanours and offences.

When our prisoner heard his name called out, he sought refuge in God.

He heard, ‘You, gendarme! Take him to his special room.’

‘Special room?’ he thought, ‘What does that mean? Is it a place where I’ll be singled out for torture?’

It was zero hour and he was about to meet him... that officer!

He could not remember how many steps he mounted or how many dark passages he passed through, but suddenly he found himself before the door of that room which he was certain would open to reveal all kinds of torments and horror.

The warder opened the door... and he could only stand and blink his sorry eyes! There was the most wonderful room opening up before him: the sun’s rays came flooding through its sparkling windows to fill the place with light. Pots of brightly coloured flowers and abundant green plants had been placed in an elegant arrangement. The sunlight interacted with the verdure of the plants to create a wonderful, relaxing feeling inside the room, while a pleasant perfume refreshed the spirits and tickled his nose. Beyond the windows could be seen some lively finches playing together and chirping happily, signalling the tone of the coming meeting.

Then, the prisoner took his first step into the room but he was immediately suspicious. He expected to see the whip waiting for him or the castle commander sitting there looking forward to meeting him. But when he saw the comfortable set up, once again he felt confused and thought that he had fallen into a new whirlpool that he would never escape from.

So, many thoughts rushed through his mind, ‘This is what I expected and feared. He’ll come to see me here, in his luxurious room. It’s your time, Officer, to take your revenge and to subject me to the worst.’

He stood beside the door awaiting his fate, and began to curse his life-style which had brought him there. Time dragged on as he thought about what might happen next. Unable to relax, he began to pace around the room; then he stood leaning against the wall, or sat on a chair beside the door. In each position, a different picture came to his mind, and he flared up in anger. His heart began to race; and his breathing became so rapid that his chest began to pump up and down out of his fear of the unknown. He stared fixedly at the door, on the alert for the slightest sound or movement that would indicate the arrival of the manager.

Suddenly, the sound of footsteps reached his ears. ‘He’s coming... He’s close to the door... He’s holding the door handle... oh God!’

Just then, the door was opened and with that the prisoner felt that his head had burst open too. He took such a deep breath that he became dizzy and his face turned ashen as though he was dying.

Our officer, Mohammad Amin, appeared before him with his face as bright as the sun; a gentle and tender smile appeared on his lips, and a noble look came to his eyes.

He greeted the prisoner, “As-Salamu alaikum wa rahmatullah!” Welcome my brother; I am so glad to receive you as a guest in this modest castle.’

He approached the prisoner, welcoming him and encircling him with his mercy just as the heavens embrace the earth and surround it.

The prisoner could not believe what was going on... he had just been greeted in the most cordial manner! It had not occurred to him to expect such a reception. He never once thought that he might expect such compassion from that man who now stood before him and overwhelmed him, and tore the fear and hatred from his heart.

Within an instant, Officer Sheikho had brought him a new sense of vitality and engulfed him with happiness and tenderness. His limbs felt like the branches of a tree that had been watered by blessed water that refreshed his spirit and given it renewed life. Moreover, the splendour of the room had not been complete until our officer entered and his presence seemed to turn it into a small Paradise where the two men sat beside one another talking face to face.

The prisoner was staring at the officer in amazement: fully absorbed in a state of deep contentment.

‘I know that I am to blame... it’s my own fault that I’m here now! I was full of hatred and contempt and intent on committing any offence to achieve my own ends! No-one forced me to do what I did... I chose to spend my life following foolish whims that led me to commit every evil and despise every favour and charity shown to me!

‘You’re such an important man, so why are you treating me with such clemency and acceptance? What stops you killing me and getting justice for yourself? By God! I cannot find any reason why you should receive me as a guest, as if I am your close friend.’

These were the thoughts going through his mind. He tried to find just one plausible reason why the officer should greet him with friendliness and extend such a warm welcome to him; why had he overwhelmed him with the care and concern which was gripping his heart and causing the firebrand inside him to die little by little, to be replaced by a spring of holy love and loyalty to him and to the Grand Omnipotent God, ‘Oh God! All my love, my praise and my passion are directed towards You for what You have directed towards me.’

It was clear that the kind treatment he received from Officer Mohammad Amin had brought joy to his heart and stopped his bad feelings. It even led him to feel deep remorse and to repent all his past evil actions. His spirit had been full of envy and bitterness, and he had gasped for personal advantage and material things, wishing to get them at any cost. And now it seemed that all of that negativity was behind him.

So, we see, quite clearly, that Mohammad Amin helped him go ahead in the way of purity. That meeting was the first step on the journey, and then it was followed by longer and greater steps. He gave up many of his own rights and pleasures for the sake of that man’s return to happiness. He spent time with him, and filled it with pleasure and kindness, and created a friendly atmosphere when in his company. He brought him tasty dishes prepared in his own home: all this to be sure that the man’s emotional and mental state improved and that he was making progress on the new journey which he had begun with him. This journey would return the prisoner to the right direction in order to adopt a new level of conduct for himself under the Benefaction of the Glorious and Praiseworthy God.

Indeed, the prisoner looked forward eagerly to every visit from Mohammad Amin and it seemed as though he had begun to be infatuated by our officer. He wished that he could stay with him all day and night to take in the sense of love that he emanated, in order to quench the thirst of his heart after the long dry years when he had turned away from God and all His Benefits. During the days he spent in the officer’s company, he lived a life full of affinity and closeness: it was a noble love, laced with gratitude, which had banished all evil intent and thoughts of sin from his spirit.

So, he understood the lesson that was given to him and learned many things from the wretched condition he passed through; he changed his mind about many things and decided to turn his back on his previous life and do away with his former despicable conduct. Therefore, God commuted his sentence and ensured that he should be released on bail after only twenty days. He came out of the prison with renewed joy in his heart and determined to think differently. He was delighted to enjoy his freedom and happiness once again, and determined to enjoy what was his and not lust after what rightfully belonged to others.

He said goodbye to the castle governor and thanked him warmly for his wonderful hospitality and personal kindness, as he knew that for the rest of his life he would be indebted to Officer Sheikho for the great favour which he had done for him.

Mohammad Amin prayed for him wholeheartedly and wished him well for the rest of his life. He emphasised that happiness and safety are achieved only by being illuminated by God’s Light, by observing His Commands and Laws, and by avoiding all those deeds that He prohibited. His last words to the man were those of the prayer, “Praise be to God, the Provider of all worlds.”

From that day on, that man adopted the right path. He kept company with the people of truth and actively became a kind and compassionate human being who wanted only God’s Satisfaction. Before he was sentenced to prison, he had done all that he could to misrepresent the illustrious aims of our officer, but as soon as he was freed he took the opposite line and did all in his power to assert that our chivalrous man was true and honest, and that every word he uttered was true and just.

In the Holy Qur’an, God says, “Goodness and Evil cannot be equal. Repel evil with what is good: then your enemy will become as close as an old and valued friend.” ﴿154﴾

This story brings to mind the memory of a great day during the age of our highest ideal, our master Mohammad (cpth): the day of the conquest of Mecca. On that day, the believers entered the city as conquerers under his leadership (cpth).

He (cpth) marched towards the city at the head of a great force of Muslims who had migrated from Mecca to enlightened Medina to escape from the non-believers and their evil leaders who had tried to put an end to his mission and to kill those who believed in him and seize their possessions. But God, the Almighty, aided His Prophet (cpth) and the believers, and it was not just a conquest but a great triumph that established the right of Islam and raised its banner above all others.

So, when our beloved master (cpth) entered Mecca, he stood before a gathering of the people and addressed them saying, ‘How should I act with you? What do you expect me to do with you?’

‘You are like a noble-minded brother to us, as was your father,’ they replied. Then, in all modesty but in full command, he said to them, ‘You can go. You are free.’

Although he was the ruler who controlled everything, and although he surely had the right and the ability to take revenge on behalf of the believers and to treat the nonbelievers as they, the believers, had been treated, this was not his purpose and he was far above such actions.

Therefore, they submitted to him and their hearts began to tend towards that humane compassion which soon overwhelmed them. Yet the noble man (cpth) did not stop at that; he also allotted the spoils gained by the Muslim army after their victory in the Battle of Hunayn ﴿155﴾

to the nonbelievers. He gave each of them two hundred camels, while he gave four hundred camels to Abu Sufyan who was their leader. He (cpth) wanted to draw Abu Sufyan closer to himself and remove all the enmity, bitterness, and darkness that was generated in his heart.

Indeed, after that, Abu Sufyan, along with his descendants, turned into beacons for Islam and became the champions of truth who spread Islam all over the world during its golden age.

The Prophet (cpth) replaced evil with good, and hatred with love, though he had no need of these people and there was no reason for him to seek their friendship. But his actions sprang from his unequalled truthfulness, wholehearted devotion, and overriding desire to uplift mankind to the appropriate level which makes them true men so that they fulfill the Trust placed in them and become deserving of their eventual return to the Gardens of Eternity.

God says, “Al’lah does call to the Home of Peace: He guides whoever wishes towards a way that is straight.” ﴿156﴾

So, the enlightened Medina is not only that of al-Hijaz, and the accomplishments did not stop after the departure of the Prophet (cpth) from this world. There is also an enlightened Medina here in al-Sham, ﴿157﴾

and glorious and illustrious feats were also performed on its land and among its people. He (cpth) said, “Seek al-Sham.”

And the Almighty called it the Holy Land for it is the place where the Godly Messages came down and is the cradle of the Prophets (cptt).

There, in your hands, is its soil; there, before your eyes, is its sky; and there its people are alive: ask them if you do not believe it!

The stones of Damascus Castle bear witness to his honour! The affirmations of his good deeds are found the length and breadth of Syria and are carried along on the waters of the great River Euphrates.

So, why do we choose the difficult way? Why do we enter a house by scaling the high walls, from where we fall? Why do we not choose the simple and obvious way, and enter a house through the door?

Perhaps our spirits are destroyed for one reason or another; perhaps we feel we can no longer stand up: then we shall spend the rest of our life creeping along the ground and buried beneath its stones.

We have been created on this earth and surely we all shall return to it. Whoever thinks that this earth is a permanent abode or place of enjoyment is foolish.

It is true that we are mortals, but we have been granted superior faculties and unrivalled powers of thought and reason that help us to become illuminated by God’s Light. When this is achieved, and only then, no-one will be given power or control over us, and only then will our wishes correspond to that which all the Prophets (cpth) have brought to mankind.

chapters.title: A Complex Story of Punishment, Rebellion and Mercy
chapters.html:
Officer Mohammad Amin held many important military posts during the French Mandate over Syria and Lebanon. At this particular time he was in charge of the central prison of Damascus Citadel and held the position of garrison commander.

Day by day, he went about his usual mundane duties but was beginning to feel frustrated and bored with the daily routine of office life; for it should be pointed out that previously in his career he had been the hero of the battlefields and accustomed to much excitement. It came as a welcome relief when the army commander phoned him and ordered him to prepare a squad of policemen under his leadership to undertake a security tour of the villages of Eastern Ghoutah ﴿158﴾

during the time of the Great Syrian Revolution.

On hearing this good news Mohammad Amin’s bad mood lifted instantly and his spirits soared with happiness, for he had been carrying out nothing but tedious office work for the past fifteen days, and had not been charged with any mission outside the citadel boundaries. It was not in his character to enjoy office work for he had always been a man of action and besides, as was mentioned, it went against his nature to indulge in a life of ease and comfort.

He wasted no time and immediately sent for his adjutant and ordered the expedition to be prepared. This was accomplished without any further delay and he was eagerly anticipating the troop’s departure, but just as he was about to mount his horse with his usual vivacity and exuberance, a soldier rushed up to inform him that the high commander was on the phone wanting to talk to him.

From Mohammad Amin’s point of view it was not good news, for the high commander asked him to remain on duty at the citadel, while his adjutant, a first lieutenant, would replace him to lead the expedition.

Our officer spoke to his superior officer in a friendly and cordial tone because of the personal connection that they had. This high commander was very fond of our officer and had a high regard for him due to his magnificent deeds; besides which he was a close friend of Mohammad Amin’s brother, General Saleem, since the general had been a superintendent of the military academy in Istanbul.

Mohammad Amin tried to persuade him to change his mind and said to him in an amiable tone, ‘Oh sir, I’m feeling quite vexed as I have been doing nothing but monotonous office work for a long time and I feel as if my soul will leave my body if I have to do it any longer. You know that I do not like it... in fact I detest it, because, as you well know, I’m much happier when I’m fighting for the security of our country or patrolling on horseback: so I request that you let me go out on patrol as you originally ordered and let my adjutant stay on duty instead of me.’

But the commander insisted on his decision and all of Mohammad Amin’s attempts aimed at making him change his mind came to nothing, and his commander then put friendship and cordiality aside and said in a frank, military tone, ‘Officer, I am giving you a military command to stay on duty at the citadel while your adjutant leads the inspection expedition... Understood?’

At this our officer became very agitated and flared up angrily saying, ‘Yes, sir! At your command!’ Slamming down the receiver, he then stormed out of his office to tell his squad there had been a change of plans and that his adjutant would now lead the patrol to Eastern Ghoutah.

He returned to his office overwhelmed by the fury erupting inside him... there was no way to escape from it or to control it. He called one of his soldiers and ordered him to bring a big block of ice, and when it was brought, he started to crush the ice with his teeth to try to cool down and find some relief from his terrible anger. But it was no use, he could not quell his rage!

There and then, he stormed out of his office, mounted his horse and left the citadel heading for his house. He cared nothing about the repercussions of his actions due to his overwhelming surge of anger, and he said to himself, ‘To hell with them and my position and the citadel!’

He pondered his situation as the sun was setting in a blaze of flaming glory, carrying its brilliant light to the west to beam on other places and other people. After a while, as the dark legions of night gradually chased away the last lingering light of the day, so did his fury steadily subside and his anger disappear. Slowly he returned to his normal state of calm, and was released from his own inner turmoil. As he began to turn the thoughts over in his mind he realised the magnitude of the great responsibilities placed on his shoulders, and how he had walked away from his position without appointing someone to take over his duties.

He knew that if anything unexpected happened with the prisoners inside the citadel, he would bear full responsibility... and he thought to himself, ‘At any rate... I should not have behaved as I did when I was angry, so I’d better go back to the citadel and get on with my work.’

There and then, he mounted his horse and went back to his office in the citadel where he settled down to carry out his duties. He began to attend to the paperwork that had accumulated on his desk during the day, and as midnight approached, the phone rang. His commanding officer was on the line in a state of extreme anxiety because of his great affection for Officer Mohammad Amin which was only strengthened by the news of a dreadful catastrophe which he had just received.

‘Are you there?’

Mohammad Amin replied, ‘Yes... I’m here... did you not order me to stay here?’ he said bitterly.

The commander added, ‘I mean did you not go with the expedition?’

He answered, ‘How could I go when you told me not to go? Then you made it a military order so I had to obey.’

The commander said, ‘I thank God that you were not with them... do you know what happened to the troop?’

‘No... no, I don’t...’ he replied.

The commander said, ‘As the expedition, led by its officers, reached the village of al-Maliha in Ghoutah (rural Damascus), they were ambushed by the rebels. The entire force, including the officers, have been captured, and so far we know nothing about them... whether they’re still alive... or dead... we have no idea what has happened to them. From the information we have we know that the inhabitants of al-Maliha village conspired with the rebels. They hosted the officers, received them hospitably, gave them food and prepared beds for them. Then, when the officers were asleep they took their firearms, and the revolutionaries went in and took all of them prisoner. And their fate is still unknown. This news was reported to us by one of our spies in the village.

‘Now what do you have to say about what I did to you... wasn’t it for your own good?’

Mohammad Amin answered him, ‘So... you had prior knowledge about it, sir... and that’s why you prevented me from going?’

The commander replied terror-stricken, ‘I seek refuge in Al’lah... no... no... far be it, and certainly not... I did not know anything.’

Then the commander seemed to writhe with fear because if it were true that he had prior knowledge of the attack, it would mean that he was a partner in the conspiracy and would certainly face execution.

Mohammad Amin said, ‘So, Al’lah is the Maker and it is He Who prevented me from being subjected to this impasse... not you.’

The General said, ‘Yes! Al’lah... Al’lah really is the Maker... The words I spoke came from my lips... but in truth they came from Him... they were His Words.’

At this point, let us go to al-Maliha village to see exactly what happened there:

When the group of policemen first reached the village, the inhabitants welcomed them warmly and received them most hospitably.

That night, the soldiers were given accommodation in various houses of the village and the officers were accommodated individually, each one in a different house. They undressed and put on their night clothes, hung their holsters on hooks on the walls. But there was trouble looming! After the guests went to sleep, feeling tranquil and honoured, they fell into the trap that had been set for them by the rebels, aided and abetted by the people of the village, who came to capture the officers one by one. Taken totally by surprise the officers could offer no resistance.

The officers were shackled with chains and their firearms became easy pickings for the rebels. They were driven barefoot and clothed in nothing but their pyjamas to the town of al-Sweida on al-Arab Mountain – where the flame of the great Syrian revolution was first sparked – to stand before Sultan Pasha al-Atrash, the head of the revolution there.

It is well known that the roads leading to al-Arab Mountain are very difficult for the traveller because they are full of rocks and thorns; and one must keep in mind that the captured officers were in chains and forced to walk barefoot. Their feet were in a terrible state, bleeding profusely, and all the while the captives were being lashed repeatedly, causing severe pain.

The officer in charge of the expedition was treated worse than the others and received the greatest share of the lashing and humiliation. He was brawny and fat, and was singled out by the leader of the rebel group for him to torment personally. He repeatedly whipped not only his back but other parts of his body, too, during the time it took for them to reach al-Sweida. Every time the lash fell on the adjutant’s back it was accompanied by obscenities because of his corpulence, in spite of the fact that this officer, one day, had tried to plead on his behalf when he was being punished by Officer Sheikho. And now, that criminal had forgotten the officer’s previous efforts on his behalf and was subjecting him to such serious torture that he lost about half of his body weight by the time they reached the rebel headquarters in al-Sweida.

After negotiations between the government of the French Mandate and the revolutionary command the captives were released in accordance with specific conditions which the two parties had agreed upon.

Let us now return to that unfortunate officer who was charged with leading the patrol in place of our officer, Mohammad Amin, and his adverse position with the leader of this rebel group which we have previously mentioned: what, exactly, was that position?

We shall relate it from the beginning:

The captive officer was an adjutant to Officer Sheikho in managing the citadel at the time. One day, the warders of the citadel seized a prisoner – who later became the most famous of the rebel leaders – and brought him to our officer after he had been caught in the act of trying to commit a hideous immoral offence with another man.

Once our officer heard of this deviation, and assured himself that it was true, he seized him by the collar and threw him to the ground in the citadel square in front of all the prisoners; then he set about whipping him and kicking him until the blood flowed from all parts of his body. Yet even this was not enough to give vent to his terrible anger, so he set about tearing the man’s skin with his teeth!

The adjutant felt such distress for the criminal that he begged his officer repeatedly to stop tormenting him, to the extent that he burst into tears of sorrow while our officer, Mohammad Amin, deaf to all entreaties, completely ignored him.

The adjutant pitied the criminal, but his great mercy stemmed from the fact that he did not know that the painful beating this criminal was suffering held mercy folded within it, although it appeared to stem from great wrath. And why should it not be so when the criminal is one of those whom Al’lah denounced when He said, “For you practise your lusts on men in preference to women: you are indeed a people transgressing beyond all limits.” ﴿159﴾

Whoever oversteps the bounds of Al’lah’s Legislation must be punished strictly, and indeed, the terrible torment now being inflicted on that criminal at the hands of this pure, chaste man is actually good and merciful as it is an attempt to save him from the jaws of degradation, moral descent, and sexual deviation. Otherwise, these terrible traits would cause him to lose all the benefits that Al’lah has prepared for him in the life to come, and would expose him to the greatest chastisement in the Hereafter if he does not repent and withdraw from his sinful ways. Therefore, it is vital that such a person should be disciplined in order to make him understand the error of his ways and make him repent. And besides, he will serve as a lesson to anyone else who is tempted to commit such an offence, and consequently the entire community will learn from the same lesson too.

Weeks and months passed as this low opportunist gradually became affiliated with the aims of the great Syrian revolution. This is a normal occurrence during any revolution or uprising, for there will always be those people – whose aims are removed from the true purpose of revolution – who sneak into its ranks, but whose aims are to achieve nothing but their own disreputable personal objectives using the principles of revolution as the means to achieve false glory. How quickly they attain their aspirations as they let no opportunity pass without seizing it to ensure that they appear as most loyal and sincere members of the revolution.

Consequently, they ascend through the levels of eminent positions through which they achieve what they will fail to attain when no longer part of it.

This is applicable to that despicable man who is now – as we have seen – a notable leader of this group of rebels, and the victim in his grasp is the same adjutant who cried out of mercy for him and who is now a captive in his hands. Does this position not seem contradictory?

But, in reality, it is not so... and the definitive proof is that the mercy which the adjutant showed for the criminal was based on sentiment and not rational thought, for he had no knowledge of the wisdom behind the beating; and so it was of no purpose to the adjutant when he came into the grasp of this criminal who subjected him to all kinds of torture.

But as for our man Mohammad Amin, although he inflicted a severe beating on the criminal, this was as a mercy upon him, for his aim was to satisfy Al’lah and to deter his wrongful and obscene behaviour. This aim led him to being in a fortified castle that safeguarded him from that criminal or, indeed, from anyone else who intended to harm him, throughout his entire life.

His only purpose in life beyond the grand deeds and great sacrifices he carried out, and which were marked by humanity and mercy was but to satisfy the Great Creator and to save His creatures, to keep them from falling, and to help them even if that resulted in infuriating mankind; therefore Al’lah helped him, supported him and preserved him – by force if necessary – from falling foul of the enemies of all that is right, and of personal enemies too, as we have seen in our story.

So, those who stay within the limits ordained by Al’lah will be protected by Him, “Al’lah is the Best to give care, and He is the Most Merciful of all those who show mercy.” ﴿160﴾

chapters.title: Part Six
chapters.html:
The French Weapons of Anjar Citadel Are Taken by Syrian Rebels

During the French occupation of Syria our officer, Mohammad Amin Sheikho, became a regional manager for Anjar Castle which was situated in the border region between Syria and Lebanon. He was appointed to this eminent position for his renowned abilities as a remarkable leader. This castle was used as a temporary arsenal for weapons being trans-shipped through Lebanon, as well as being an important centre and stronghold against the Syrian insurgents.

It happened that the French government sent a large consignment of various kinds of weapons and ammunition to supply its military forces in Syria and Lebanon who were tasked with suppressing the insurgency and other minor uprisings wherever they broke out.

The consignment of war materiel was shipped from France and transported to the castle in the border territory where it was stored pending its distribution to the French forces in Syria.

When the shipment arrived at Anjar Castle the weapons became the sole responsibility of the officer who was in charge of the security of the castle.

Despite having been entrusted with such a high position by the French, Officer Sheikho’s loyalties lay with the rebels who were fighting to liberate their country. And so, he resolved to deliver the weapons to the Syrian insurgents, who were the enemies of the French government, even though he risked losing his own life for what the French would see as the worst possible betrayal.

He duly informed the insurgents and instructed them to start removing the arms under the cover of darkness. Accordingly, he gave leave of absence to some policemen whom he felt unable to trust and told his loyal men to remain on duty along with his faithful adjutant. When night fell and darkness prevailed, the rebels came and began to remove the weapons from the castle under cover of the dark, cloudy sky.

After midnight, the ingenious officer called the commanderin- chief to tell him that the castle had come under attack by a large and powerful force of rebels, ‘The castle’s under attack... my men are fighting back bravely but they’re outnumbered... it’s a major skirmish... the rebels are bent on breaking into the castle, so... hurry... send reinforcements...!’

He had previously ordered his policemen to fire continuously into the air for the local villagers to hear; and he had arranged with the mayor of the village to say that he, Officer Sheikho, had actually sought his help, but that he was unable to offer any assistance because he lacked fighting power as the villagers were merely unarmed farmers. When the French forces, which Officer Sheikho had purposely summoned too late, arrived at the castle, they found that the rebels had emptied the storerooms of every last weapon and piece of ammunition, and had escaped with their spoils, successfully and safely.
